cues.text: You signed up to watch one show.
There was a free trial, the show looked good, and getting started took less than a minute.
A week later, you've finished watching.
You open your account, find the subscription, and decide to cancel.
The first page asks if you're sure.
The next reminds you what you'll lose.
Then there's another offer, another button, and another page.
At some point, you may wonder if you've cancelled already, or if you've just told the website that you're thinking about cancelling.
Some subscriptions are easy to end.
But when leaving takes more effort than joining, that extra effort can have a financial value to the company collecting the payments.
To understand why, start with what made the subscription convenient.
When you rent a movie, you pay, watch it, and the transaction ends.
An automatically renewing subscription keeps going until something changes.
Your music doesn't stop every month while you hunt for your card.
The company gets a more predictable income and you skip another checkout.
